phonemes.desc: The first syllable: an unrounded 'hwa' with rounded lips from the rounded medial, carrying primary stress in the romanised form.
The second syllable, short and level in the Korean reading, closing in a simple nasal.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HWAH-neen' — in the Korean reading the first syllable is pronounced with rounded lips and the second is short and level. The scholarly form Hwanin preserves the capital that marks a proper name; the ASCII form hananim is an older romanisation still used in domain names.

kin.label: Korean vernacular
kin.form: Hananim (하나님), the native reading later adopted as the Korean Christian name for God (Grayson, Korea: A Religious History)

pronunciation.note: Hwanin is Tier 2: the scholarly restoration preserves only the capital marking a proper name — no distinctive diacritic or non-ASCII letter distinguishes it from the ASCII 'hananim'. The Hangul 환인 and Hanja 桓因 carry the meaning the Latin form cannot show.

domains.title: Hwanin, Lord of Heaven
domains.subtitle: the supreme source of the Dangun founding myth
domains.lead: Hwanin is the supreme celestial figure who rules from heaven in the Dangun founding myth in Korean tradition. The name means "Lord of Heaven" and belongs to the domain "Supreme God, Heaven." In the Samguk Yusa, Hwanin is the ruler of heaven who answers his son Hwanung's wish for the earth by choosing the sacred site and sending him down with three thousand retainers and the heavenly seals of authority. Hwanin is not a creator in the biblical sense; he is the apex of a celestial hierarchy that authorises the descent of culture and law to the Korean peninsula.

cards.name: Lord of Heaven
cards.desc: Hwanin sits at the apex of the Korean celestial order, the source from which legitimate authority descends.

cards.name: Celestial Court
cards.desc: Heaven is imagined as a court with ministers, retainers, and an ethical law that mirrors human government.

cards.name: Ancestor of Hwanung
cards.desc: Hwanin authorises the descent that makes possible the birth of Dangun and the founding of Korea.

cards.name: Moral Order
cards.desc: The myth encodes the belief that rulers and peoples are accountable to a higher heavenly standard.

symbols.name: The heavens
symbols.meaning: The celestial realm from which Hwanin dispenses authority and blessing.

symbols.name: The sandalwood tree
symbols.meaning: The axis linking heaven and earth in the Dangun myth; the place where Hwanung alighted on Taebaeksan.

symbols.name: The heavenly seal
symbols.meaning: The token of delegated authority that Hwanin gives to Hwanung — the warrant without which the descent is illegitimate.

symbols.name: Sun and moon
symbols.meaning: Celestial emblems of the luminous, ordering presence of heaven.

symbols.name: Mugwort and garlic
symbols.meaning: The hundred-day food of the bear-woman — the austere diet that turns a beast into the ancestress of the Korean people.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Hwanin survives in a single late masterpiece: the Samguk Yusa ('Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms') of the monk Iryeon, compiled in 1281 CE from much older Korean and Chinese materials. In it, Hwanin — explicitly identified with Indra, the Buddhist lord of heaven — sends his son Hwanung down beneath a sandalwood tree, and from that descent flow the tiger-and-bear transformation, the birth of Dangun, and the whole legitimating myth of Korea's foundation.

myths.title: The Lord of Heaven Sends His Son
myths.text: Iryeon's Samguk Yusa opens the Korean story with Hwanin, 桓因, whom the text itself glosses as Indra — the Buddhist Śakra, lord of the thirty-three heavens. When his son Hwanung, 桓雄, gazed down upon the human world and asked to rule it, Hwanin looked down in turn, chose the fairest spot under heaven, and fixed there the sacred altar. He gave his son three heavenly seals and a retinue of three thousand, and Hwanung descended beneath a sandalwood tree on Taebaeksan, bearing the tokens of rule, the arts of law, grains, and medicine. (Iryeon, Samguk Yusa, 'Gojoseon' chapter, trans. Ha and Mintz, pp. 32–41.) The myth is striking because heaven is bureaucratic as well as holy: authority travels downward from father to son, sealed and documented, so that Korean kingship arrives on earth already carrying heaven's warrant.

myths.title: The Tiger and the Bear
myths.text: Living beneath the sandalwood tree, Hwanung was approached by a tiger and a she-bear who begged him to make them human. The god gave them twenty cloves of garlic and a bundle of mugwort and set a single condition: eat only this and shun the sunlight for one hundred days. The tiger could not endure the discipline and fled back to the wilds; the bear persevered, and on the twenty-first day she shed her fur and became a woman, Ungnyeo — the bear-woman. Childless, she prayed beneath the tree, and Hwanung took her as his wife. She bore a son, Wanggeom, 'the prince of the sandalwood,' whom heaven chose as the first king of the Korean people: Dangun. (Samguk Yusa, 'Gojoseon.') The tale ranks patience above strength: the beast that submits to law and time becomes the ancestress of a nation, while the stronger animal is forgotten.

myths.title: Dangun's Fifteen Centuries
myths.text: Dangun Wanggeom, child of the bear-woman and the son of heaven, founded Gojoseon — 'Old Joseon' — in 2333 BCE by the myth's traditional dating, and ruled for fifteen hundred years. When his time on earth was done he did not die as mortals die: he returned to the mountains and became a god of the peaks, Asadal, the spirit who still presides over the land he governed. Iryeon adds that Dangun's priests, the Jeceon, 'worship heaven' at his shrine, tying the ancestral cult directly to the heaven that sent him. The myth's grand claim is easy to miss: Korean kingship is not a human invention or a conquest but a family inheritance, carried down through Hwanin and Hwanung and never surrendered — its founder still holds the mountains in trust for his descendants.

myths.title: Hwanin Re-Dressed by Every Age
myths.text: A second layer of the story shows the myth being rewritten by each age that tells it. On the page of the Samguk Yusa, Hwanin is Indra — the Sanskrit Śakra — so the heavenly father of the Korean foundation arrives wearing Buddhist cosmology. Later readers re-dressed the same descent in Confucian costume as a model of ethical hierarchy, and in 1909 the nationalist religion Daejonggyo installed Dangun, and through him the heaven that sent him, at the center of a modern faith. Twentieth-century scholarship treated the tale as a charter myth of Gojoseon, while North and South Korea both canonized it — in schoolbooks and on National Foundation Day — as the beginning of the nation. The myth survives precisely by surrendering its details: every generation re-clothes the same descent of heaven's authority in the costume of its own dominant thought.

etymology.derivation: The name is composed of the Sino-Korean elements 桓 (hwan, "spreading, majestic") and 因 (in, "cause, origin"). Read 환인 in Korean, it denotes the supreme celestial authority in the Dangun myth cycle.

nameVariations.note: Scholarly romanisation of 桓因, the form used in the Samguk Yusa.
Korean vernacular reading; later adopted as the Christian name for God.
Hangul form corresponding to the Hanja 桓因.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Hwanin, the Hangul form is 환인 and the Hanja form is 桓因. Hangul ‘환인’ and Hanja ‘桓因’, the forms used in the Samguk Yusa; the name is also rendered ‘Hananim’ (하나님) in Korean vernacular usage. The ASCII form hananim is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Hwanin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Hwanin entered Korean religion on two tracks at once. The Samguk Yusa itself glosses Hwanin as Indra — the Buddhist Śakra, lord of heaven — folding the Korean celestial father into the Sanskrit cosmology that Buddhism carried east. In the twentieth century the vernacular title Hananim became the standard Korean Christian name for God, so that Protestant congregations prayed to a word that had once named the father of Hwanung. In shamanic and nationalist discourse Hwanin remains the mythic ancestor of the Korean people; the Daejonggyo movement, founded in 1909, worshipped Dangun and, through him, the heaven that sent him. Confucian interpreters read the celestial hierarchy as an ethical model of good government. All these traditions keep one constant: Korea's legitimacy descends from heaven, whatever costume the Lord of Heaven wears.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hwanin survives in Korean public life chiefly through the Dangun myth, which is taught in schools, celebrated on National Foundation Day (Gaecheonjeol, 3 October), and invoked in discussions of Korean identity on both sides of the peninsula. The name Hananim remains one of the most common words for God in Korean Christianity — it is the word Korean Bibles print for the biblical God — while Hwanin continues to appear in scholarly reconstructions of early Korean religion, in museum exhibitions on Gojoseon, and in cultural diplomacy that presents Korea as a nation with ancient, heaven-blessed foundations.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hwanin is a god known almost entirely through his absence from the story he frames. He never descends; he appoints, seals, and sends. The active divine work of the Korean foundation myth is done by his son and grandson — Hwanung who rules beneath the sandalwood tree, Dangun who founds the state — while Hwanin remains above, the unmoved source of a moved world. That structure is the myth's theology in miniature: heaven does not administer the earth directly but delegates, authorizes, and watches, and legitimacy on the peninsula is real only insofar as it can trace that delegation back upward to its source.

The restoration of the name matters in the same register. 'Hananim' in ASCII flattens a title — the Lord of Heaven, 환인, 桓因 — into a string a registrar can process; Hwanin restores the capital, the characters, and the centuries-old claim that a Korean word can carry the highest meaning in the language: the Christian God, the shamanic ancestor, and the bureaucratic father of kings all live inside it at once.

lore.archaeology: Because Hwanin belongs to a late-written myth rather than an excavated cult, his 'archaeology' is the archaeology of the myth's own survival and projection. The Samguk Yusa survives in early manuscripts of 1390 and 1512; the Dangun narrative it records was projected backward into art by the Goguryeo tomb murals of the fourth–sixth centuries CE, where celestial courts, sun-and-moon deities, and sacred-tree imagery painted on the ceilings of the Ji'an-area tombs give visual form to the same heavenly order that sends a son down to earth. In modern times the association of the myth's 'sacred sandalwood' with the slopes of Baekdusan — inferred, not stated, from the Samguk Yusa's Taebaeksan — has fixed Hwanin's descent-point on the peninsula's most symbolically charged mountain, and Dangun's traditional tomb is maintained as a shrine near Pyongyang, visited by Koreans from both North and South.
